content: 1. After removing the outer boot, step away from the coverall and dispose of it safely. If the outer gloves are removed before the coverall, perform additional hand hygiene as outlined in the protocol. 2. Remove eye protection by pulling the strap from behind the head while keeping your eyes closed, and dispose of it safely. 3. Perform hand hygiene on gloved hands after removing eye protection. 4. Remove the mask by first untying the bottom strap above the head and letting it hang in front, then untie the top strap from behind the head. Keep your eyes closed during this process, and dispose of the mask safely. 5. Decontaminate boots thoroughly, ensuring all sides and the bottom are cleaned. Move to a lower-risk area one foot at a time. If removing the boots, avoid touching them directly and perform additional hand hygiene on gloved hands. 6. Carefully remove gloves using the appropriate technique to avoid contamination, and dispose of them safely. 7. Non-disposable aprons must be disinfected by the wearer. This includes cleaning to remove visible contamination, disinfection, and hanging the apron to dry outside the changing room in sunlight. 8. Goggles or face shields must fit securely and comfortably. Each individual should have their own goggles or face shield, labeled with their name. Goggles should be disinfected with a 0.5% chlorine solution for 10 minutes, washed with water, and dried outside the changing room. Anti-fog spray can be applied to minimize condensation, which can impair vision. 9. Gloves are effective in preventing contamination of healthcare workers’ hands and reducing pathogen transmission. However, gloves do not provide complete protection, as pathogens can access hands through small defects in the gloves or during glove removal. Hand hygiene remains essential after glove removal. 10. Medical gloves are single-use items and should not be reprocessed or reused, even in resource-limited settings. 11. Spraying disinfectants in clinical areas, whether occupied or unoccupied, is discouraged by WHO. This practice has no proven disease control benefit and may aerosolize the virus, posing risks to staff and patients. Spraying should only be considered in specific outdoor or community settings, such as decontaminating Ebola victims’ households or disinfecting sand or gravel floors. 12. Common PPE mistakes include exposing wrists during wide movements, touching goggles with contaminated gloves, removing goggles prematurely, and improper handling of medical glasses during goggle removal. 13. Healthcare workers should follow the flow from less contaminated to more contaminated areas within the red zone. Staff must respect the flow from suspected to probable to confirmed wards. 14. All healthcare workers and ETU staff should have their temperatures checked daily upon arrival at the ETU. If a worker is sick, they should stay home and notify their supervisor. Occupational health infrastructure, such as a small clinic, should be available for workers to report illnesses and exposures. 15. Healthcare workers should avoid sharing personal items, maintain physical distancing, and refrain from informal care of sick colleagues or family members during outbreaks. They should also avoid working simultaneously in non-Ebola health facilities to reduce the risk of infection. 16. Discharge of patients should follow specific criteria, including clinical improvement, absence of significant symptoms, and negative blood PCR tests for VHF. Patients should be counseled and provided with follow-up care plans. 17. Discharged patients may face stigmatization and rejection in their communities. Psychosocial support and community awareness activities should accompany discharge to address these challenges. 18. Male Ebola survivors and their sexual partners should receive counseling on safe sexual practices until their semen tests negative for the virus twice. Survivors should be provided with condoms and instructions for their use for at least three months after symptom onset. Semen testing should be offered at three months and monthly thereafter until two consecutive negative results are obtained. 19. Survivors should be counseled on the prevention of HIV, other STIs, and unplanned pregnancies. If PCR testing is unavailable, safe sex practices should continue for at least 12 months, with adjustments based on emerging data. 20. Discharged patients should receive a medical certificate confirming they pose no danger to their families or communities. Survivors should also be provided with documentation of their treatment and recovery to facilitate continuity of care in outpatient settings.
